text: Somatic cells in mammalian semen can be a potential source of nuclei for nuclear transfer to produce cloned animals. Somatic cells recovered from avian semen could also provide a source of cells for use in chimera formation or cloning of threatened and endangered birds. This type of assisted reproductive technology is especially important when a genetically unique animal has died and the only viable genetic material available is semen cryopreserved for artificial insemination and in vitro fertilization purposes. The usefulness of somatic cells obtained from fresh and frozen mammalian semen for nuclear transfer has already been evaluated, but still remains to be accomplished for avian semen. A non-invasive, or minimally invasive, technique to conserve avian genetic diversity via somatic cell collection from fresh avian semen, to our knowledge, has not been described. The present study investigated the use of fresh semen samples from domestic chickens (Gallus domesticus) (n = 7), i.e., white leghorn (n = 4) and silkie chickens (n = 3), as a source of somatic cells, specifically fibroblast-like cells and epithelial cells, for cytological analysis and somatic cell gene banking. Ultimately, somatic cell culture was successful for two of six selected samples (33.3%), with two of four white leghorn semen samples yielding cell cultures compared to 0 of 2 silkie chicken semen samples. Further research may include applying this technique to other avian species or address the effects of cryopreservation on the viability and DNA integrity of somatic cells derived in this manner.

Somatic cells found in human semen include epithelial cells, and various major leukocyte subpopulations such as granulocytes, monocytes/macrophages, B lymphocytes, helper and suppressor/cytotoxic T lymphocytes (Phillips et al., 1978;Wolff and Anderson, 1988;Homyk et al., 1990). However, limited information is available about somatic cells in semen of livestock and companion animals. Phillips et al. (1978) reported that epithelial cultures, uncontaminated by fibroblast cells, were obtained from human semen samples. More recently, epithelial cell cultures have been obtained from eland (Nel-Themaat et al., 2007) and sheep (Liu et al., 2009) semen. However, to our knowledge the question of whether or not somatic cells can be isolated and cultured from avian semen samples has not been addressed.
Semen contains somatic cells that are a potential source of nuclei for nuclear transfer to produce genetically identical animals. For instance, some animals of high genetic value have died and the only viable genetic material available is cryopreserved semen. As has been demonstrated with bovine semen (Liu et al., 2010), growing somatic cells from fresh samples provides the knowledge to eventually be able to grow somatic cells from frozen semen. Somatic cells recovered from semen samples in this manner can be used for cytological analysis and possibly for cloning and chimera formation. If somatic cells in semen can be used successfully for somatic nuclear transfer (SCNT), then this could, in some cases, represent an extremely valuable resource for the preservation or restoration of these valuable animals. The recovery of somatic cells, specifically, epithelial cells and fibroblast-like cells (hereafter referred to as fibroblast cells), from avian semen would in effect allow for the non-invasive collection of somatic cells for cytogenetic analysis and for use in techniques such as chimera formation, iPSC creation, or cloning. The primary objective of the present investigation was to determine if a method developed for recovering mammalian somatic cells from fresh semen could be applied for isolating and propagating somatic cells from freshly collected avian semen.

Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium/Nutrient Mixture F-12 (DMEM/F-12) was purchased from Gibco (Grand Island, NY, USA). Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was purchased from Hyclone (Logan, UT, USA). All other reagents were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO, USA) unless otherwise indicated.

section: semen collection, transport, somatic cell isolation, and culture
text:
The research herein was conducted in accordance with the Animal Care Guidelines of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Texas A&M University. Chickens were caged at a minimum density of one hen per cage, 216 inches 2 per bird, each cage having its own nipple drinker providing a readily available water supply. All feeds were manufactured at a mill located at the poultry center and formulated using current NRC (Nutritional Requirements of Chickens) guidelines. The birds were fed a standard laying mash consisting of roughly 17% protein, 3.6% calcium, and 2,866 kcal kg -1 . For internal and external parasite control, the feed contained Monensin (Coban 60, 60 active grams per ton). External parasites, such as northern fowl mites, poultry lice, and insects were controlled with a 10% permethyrin spray (Permasan). Seven ejaculates were collected from white leghorn chickens (n = 4) and silkie chickens (n = 3), at the Poultry Science Research, Teaching, and Extension Center at Texas A&M University. Two of the seven ejaculates were pooled due to small volumes, i.e., two silkie chicken semen samples, thereby producing six separate samples. All of the animals appeared to be in good health at the time of the semen collections.
Semen was expressed via manual massaging of the rooster's abdomen; similar to the method described previously in Gee et al. (2004) and Quinn and Burrows (1936). Before beginning the massage technique, feathers were trimmed away from the cloaca and the area was washed using 70% isopropyl alcohol. The semen was expelled and collected in a 10 mL glass beaker and diluted approximately 1:3 with 0.9% phosphate buffered saline (PBS) solution before transferring the sample to a 15 mL conical tube. Then, the semen sample was placed in a Styrofoam cooler with an ice pack in the bottom, and separated by a paper towel, for transport (~15 min) and subsequent preparation for processing in the laboratory.
Somatic cells were isolated and cultured as described in Liu et al. (2009) and Nel-Themaat et al. (2008a;b) with minor modifications. Briefly, each semen sample was gently layered over a 3-layer gradient column (2.5 mL each of 20%, 50%, and 90% Percoll®) in a 15 mL conical tube and centrifuged at 400g for 20 min. Cells in the 20% gradient and top half of the 50% gradient were centrifuged at least twice at 400g for 10 min. in DMEM/F12 supplemented with 100 µg mL -1 gentamicin by centrifugation. Afterwards, cell pellets were re-suspended in DMEM/F-12 supplemented with 10% FBS, 10 ng mL -1 epidermal growth factor, 30 µg mL -1 bovine pituitary extract, 5 µg mL -1 insulin, 10 ng mL -1 cholera toxin, 200 µg mL -1 gentamycin, 100 units mL -1 penicillin, 100 µg mL -1 streptomycin, and 0.25 µg mL -1 amphotericin B, and cultured in 25 cm 2 (T-25) cell culture flasks (BD Falcon, Franklin Lakes, NJ, USA) with vent caps (2µm pore size) at 37 ºC in a humidified atmosphere of 5% CO 2 in air. Medium was changed 24 h after plating.
The cell culture flasks were checked for bacteria and/or fungi contamination daily for one week. Medium in cell culture flasks containing bacteria and/or fungi was replaced with fresh medium until contamination was eliminated. The concentration of gentamicin was decreased at each medium change from 150 µg mL -1 to 100 µg mL -1 , and finally to 50 µg mL -1 . Penicillin, streptomycin, and amphotericin B were likewise gradually excluded from the culture medium (within one to two weeks of culture). Cells were fed twice a week with fresh medium until cell culture could be verified as successful and documented using an inverted confocal microscope (Nikon Instruments Inc., Melville, NY, USA) with a fluorescence light source, 100x to 400x magnification, and NIS Elements imaging software.

The total number of cells obtained from each ejaculate varied, but somatic cell numbers were low and this may be due to the isolation procedure requiring further modifications in future research efforts. Basically, either no cell attachment was found (n = 3, 50%) or a few cells per ejaculate attached and started to divide (n = 3, 50%), however, one of these aforementioned cell cultures was discarded due to bacterial contamination, the silkie chicken sample. Ultimately, fibroblast cell growth was successfully obtained from two of the six samples cultured (33.3%), both from white leghorn chicken samples (Figures 1 and2). The somatic cell cultures typically initiated with bacteria and/or fungi contamination and this issue contributed to lower cell culture success.
Comparing the white leghorn chicken semen samples, only two of four provided somatic cells versus one of two for silkie chickens. In terms of somatic cell culture, two of four white leghorn chicken semen samples yielded somatic cell cultures versus zero of two silkie chicken semen samples.

Isolating and propagating somatic cells from frozen semen can be difficult, especially when there are a limited number of semen straws/pellets. However, perhaps nuclei of the somatic cells in frozen semen could be used for nuclear transfer even though the cell membrane and cytoplasm might be damaged as a result of the semen cryopreservation process. It is expected that the ease of obtaining somatic cells from semen samples will vary depending upon the method used for semen collection, e.g., the propensity for somatic cells to slough off into the semen during collection given the collection technique being utilized, as well as the size of the avian species being collected and the relative semen volume obtained.  In the present study, small numbers of somatic cells were obtained from each ejaculate; as such, perhaps the isolation procedure may require modification in an attempt to increase the number of somatic cells isolated in future efforts. Notably, the semen sample sizes in the present study are not very large, n = 4 and n = 2 for white leghorn and silkie chickens, respectively, thereby negating the use of a statistical analysis regarding somatic cell culture success between breeds. More replicates with larger sample sizes in a future study could provide an adequate statistical power for examining the influence of breeds on the success of somatic cell isolation and cell culture.
Similar to Liu et al. (2010), although the genital area, in this case the cloaca area of the chickens, was cleaned before each semen collection; bacteria and/or fungi contamination remained a problem when growing these cells in culture. This is likely to be even more of an issue with avian semen collections due to the differences in physiology compared to animals where the semen is expressed separately from the area where the excrement also passes. We found that at 24 h post plating, a gentle washing (using culture medium) of the culture surface to which cells might have attached, helped remove bacteria and fungi; thereby decreasing the concentrations of antibiotics required in the culture medium and increasing the chances of obtaining cell growth. Perhaps more frequent medium changes during the first 24 to 72 h post plating would have helped prevent bacterial contamination as reported by Liu et al. (2010).

In the present study, we have demonstrated that somatic cells, specifically epithelial cells and fibroblast cells, can be isolated and cultured from fresh avian ejaculates. Some of the somatic cells cultured from avian semen ejaculates exhibited epithelial cell morphology, similar to the results found in Bos taurus (Liu et al., 2010). Unlike the case in Liu et al. (2010), where somatic cell growth was obtained from fresh bovine ejaculates with relatively high efficiency, it was not the case in the present study.
More specifically, the results demonstrate that domestic chicken semen can be a non-invasive, or minimally invasive, source of somatic cells for cell culture and as such serve for subsequent cytogenetic analysis or perhaps even for such techniques as iPSC creation. This also means that avian semen can possibly provide a source of somatic cells for chimera formation or perhaps even for future avian cloning with a special focus on critically endangered birds, e.g., Spix's macaw (Cyanopsitta spixii) or the Grenada dove (Leptotila wellsi).
Additional research on obtaining somatic cells from avian semen and refining the aforementioned cell culture technique appears warranted given the potential value of this approach for improving genetic diversity. In the future, research should be conducted on isolating somatic cells from cryopreserved avian semen of different species for assessing post-thaw cell viability and DNA integrity.

Noninvasive genetic census of greater one-horned rhinoceros Rhinoceros unicornis in Gorumara National Park, India: a pilot study for population estimation U D A Y A

The greater one-horned rhinoceros Rhinoceros unicornis is a flagship species for conservation in protected areas in India and Nepal. In India the species is afforded the highest level of legal protection under Schedule I of the Wildlife (Protection) Act . Although censuses of greater one-horned rhinoceros have been carried out for decades using the traditional total count method, no advanced scientific approach has been adopted for population estimation of the species in India or elsewhere. We optimized noninvasive genetic techniques for identification of greater one-horned rhinoceros from dung samples, and applied these to estimate the number of rhinoceros in Gorumara National Park, in West Bengal, India. Our results confirmed the presence of  individuals from  dung samples collected throughout the Park in . We confirmed a maleto-female sex ratio of . : , based on analysis of DNA from dung samples, using a y-chromosome linked marker. Our results are in concordance with a census carried out by the West Bengal Forest Department that found  rhinoceros in the Park, with a male-to-female sex ratio of . : . Our study thus demonstrates the feasibility of using a noninvasive genetic approach for population estimation of greater one-horned rhinoceros in the wild.

T he greater one-horned rhinoceros Rhinoceros unicornis is a Schedule I species under India's Wildlife (Protection) Act , and is categorized as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List (IUCN, ). The species was once distributed throughout the northern floodplains and the Himalayan foothills of the Indian subcontinent, between the Indo-Myanmar border in the east and Pakistan's Sindhu river basin in the west (Rao, ; Laurie et al., ; Leader-Williams, ) but as a result of habitat destruction and poaching for its horn it is now confined to a few isolated patches in protected areas in India and Nepal (Laurie et al., ; Talukdar et al., ). The Indian population of greater one-horned rhinoceros accounts for . % of the global population of the species (Talukdar et al., ) and is spread across seven protected areas: Kaziranga National Park, Orang National Park, Pobitora Wildlife Sanctuary and Manas National Park in the state of Assam, Gorumara National Park and Jaldapara National Park in the state of West Bengal, and Dudhwa National Park in the state of Uttar Pradesh.
Accurate estimation of population size is of paramount importance in the conservation and management of threatened species, to assess conservation needs and evaluate effects of conservation actions (Gese, ). Population monitoring of white rhinoceros Ceratotherium simum and black rhinoceros Diceros bicornis in Africa has been carried out using various techniques, including identification based on distinct body features (Conway & Goodman, ; Kiwia, ; Walpole et al., ; Patton et al., ), radio-tagging (Galli & Flamand, ), spoor (Alibhai et al., ) and camera-trapping (Stein et al., ), aerial counts from aircraft, using multiple observers (Brockett, ; Ngene et al., ), and counts at water holes, using photographic records (Cilliers, ). In Nepal, photographs of individual onehorned rhinoceros have been used to estimate the minimum population size in Chitwan National Park (Laurie, ; Dinerstein & Price, ). Rhinoceros populations have also been monitored by observers riding elephants, using a total block count method to identify individual rhinoceros based on features such as horn shape, skin folds and body marks (Subedi et al., ). In India the rhinoceros has been censused using a total count method, whereby rhinoceros are counted by observers riding elephants; multiple teams count the total number of individuals observed in assigned blocks, which are generally demarcated by physical boundaries such as rivers, streams or roads (Lahan & Sonowal, ). Unlike the block count method used in Nepal, the total count method adopted in India does not strictly employ individual identification based on distinct body features.
In recent years noninvasive genetic approaches have emerged as an alternative to invasive capture-mark-recapture methods, providing an opportunity to identify individuals without the need to capture, harm or disturb them (Taberlet et al., , ; Kohn et al., ; Smith et al., ; Borthakur et al., ). There are a number of potential benefits to genetic tagging compared with physical tagging (Taberlet et al., ), including an increase in the number of records (yielding more accurate estimates), reduced stress and mortality, reduced capture bias caused by trap response, and a shorter sampling period to approximate closure better (Miller et al., ). The estimation of population size by means of noninvasive genetic sampling and capture-mark-recapture models is a complex multistep process, which involves an appropriate sampling design (Lindberg & Rexstad, ; Boulanger et al., ), effective field techniques, a reliable protocol of individual identification (Paetkau, ), and adequate capture-mark-recapture modelling for population estimation (Mondol et al., ).
We conducted a genetic-tagging-based census of greater one-horned rhinoceros in Gorumara National Park. Our objective was to optimize protocols for genetic identification from dung samples so that this approach, with development of a robust sampling strategy, could be used for geneticbased estimation of the population size of the species in the wild across India.

The c.  km  Gorumara National Park lies in the floodplains of the Murti and Raidak rivers, in the state of West Bengal (Fig. ). This region is part of the Eastern Himalayan submontane Terai belt and the Indo-Malayan ecozone. Gorumara was chosen as the study site because of its known small population of rhinoceros ( individuals), with a male-to-female sex ratio of . :  (according to the March  census conducted by West Bengal Forest Department using the total count method).

Technical details of the genetic analysis are provided as Supplementary Material.
Field survey and sample collection The field survey was undertaken during April  by UB and PKD accompanied by the field staff of Gorumara Forest Department, to locate fresh samples of rhinoceros dung, preferably deposited no more than  hours prior to collection. Elephants were used throughout the survey for transportation in areas that could not be accessed by vehicles. Circa - g of dung from each sample was collected in plastic vials containing DMSO-EDTA-Trissalt saturated (DETs) buffer. The geographical coordinates of each sample were recorded using a global positioning system. We collected  samples of rhinoceros dung from Gorumara National Park during April  (Fig. ). We also extracted DNA from  reference tissue samples from dead rhinoceros, collected during - and preserved in % ethanol, for use in marker standardization. All samples were kept at a temperature of -°C prior to DNA extraction.
DNA extraction DNA was extracted from dung samples using the guanidine isothiocyanate-silica-based protocol (Boom et al., ), with modifications (see Supplementary Material for full details). All DNA extractions were performed in a room dedicated for low-quality DNA work. DNA extractions from reference tissues and samples were performed using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue kit (QIAGEN, Hilden, Germany), following standard kit protocols. one-horned rhinoceros to determine the level of polymorphism. The selected polymorphic loci (Table ) were used to genotype the samples of rhinoceros dung. We used a multiple tube approach (Taberlet et al., ), assigning quality indices to the genotype data, following Miquel et al. () for genotyping quality control and assessment of genotyping error (see Supplementary Material for full details).

We used Ychromosome-specific SRY (sex-determining region of the Y chromosome) primers designed from horse SRY sequences (primers were designed at the Center for Conservation and Research of Endangered Wildlife, Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden, USA). Microsatellite locus SRIIIA (- bp) was used as nuclear control in a multiplex reaction with the SRY ( bp) marker to distinguish between PCR failures and female samples in a single-tube PCR. Male samples were identified by the presence of both SRY and SRIIIA PCR products, and female samples were identified by the presence of only SRIIIA products (see Supplementary Material for full details).

Three of the  microsatellite loci on the reference tissue samples (SR, SR and SR) were found to be monomorphic (Table ). The observed heterozygosity was -. across the  loci, and the mean values of expected and observed heterozygosity were . and ., respectively. The PCR success rate was % for all loci; no allelic dropout or false alleles were observed for any of the loci in reference samples. Three of the loci, SR (χ  = ., df = , P , .), SRIIIA (χ  = ., df = , P , .) and Rh (χ  = ., df = , P , .), were found to deviate significantly from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, with no linkage disequilibrium. On the basis of the three criteria described in the Methods,  polymorphic loci were selected for genotyping the rhinoceros dung samples. The cumulative values of probability of identity and probability of identity among siblings of these  loci were found to be as low as . •  - and . •  - , respectively, which indicates the high resolving power of these loci in the identification of individual rhinoceros. Figure  is a graphical representation of the cumulative values of probability of identity and probability of identity among siblings for all  loci, in increasing order of single locus value, for the  reference samples.
In accordance with quality index criteria, genotype data for  dung samples were retained for identification of unique multilocus genotypes and determination of the number of individual rhinoceros. The number of alleles, allele size range, percentage PCR success, allelic dropout, false alleles, and expected and observed heterozygosity for the  microsatellite loci in the  samples are presented in Table . Locus Rh was found to be monomorphic in the Gorumara population. The observed heterozygosity was -. across the  loci, and mean expected and observed values were . and ., respectively. PCR success was -% across the  loci, and an overall genotyping error rate of % was observed. The cumulative probability of identity and probability of identity among siblings were . •  - and . •  - , respectively. Figure  is a graphical representation of the cumulative values of probability of identity and probability of identity among siblings for the  polymorphic loci, in increasing order of single locus value, for the  dung samples. Significant deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium was observed in six loci: Rh (χ  = ., df = , P , .), Rh (χ  = ., df = , P , .), Rh (χ  = ., df= , P, .), Rh (χ  = ., df = , P , .), Rh (χ  = ., df = , P , .) and SR (χ  = ., df = , P , .). No linkage disequilibrium was observed in any of the loci in the  dung samples. Individual identity analysis yielded  unique multilocus genotypes in the  samples, confirming the presence of  individual rhinoceros in Gorumara during the sampling period. Identification of unique multilocus genotypes based on zero and single locus mismatch yielded the same number of individuals. Sex identification analysis indicated there were  male and nine female rhinoceros (a male-to-female sex ratio of .:).

We used noninvasive genetic techniques to identify individual greater one-horned rhinoceros in Gorumara National Park. The  microsatellite loci selected indicated low probability of identity (. •  - ) and probability of identity among siblings of . •  - for the dung samples collected. These values are comparable to those found in other studies (Vidya et al., ; Flagstad et al., ). The cut-off number of loci for individual identification was a trade-off between a high probability of identity and increasing risk of introducing higher genotyping error by additional loci, as suggested in other studies (Borthakur et al., ; Flagstad et al., ).
Quality index criteria allowed % of samples to be retained for final analysis, which is a higher proportion than in other studies (e.g. Flagstad et al., ). Using a quality index cut-off value of . retained % of samples of elephant dung stored in ethanol; Borthakur et al. (), using a quality index cut-off value of ., retained only % of In  the West Bengal Forest Department counted  rhinoceros in Gorumara, with a male-to-female sex ratio of . :  (Department of Environment, Government of West Bengal). Our results are similar ( and . : , respectively). The genetic-based total count is practical and cost effective for small populations such as in Gorumara, where obtaining samples from every rhinoceros is possible. A comparative analysis of the costs involved in the genetic-based total count and traditional total count methods is not within the scope of this study, however, because data for the latter are unavailable. Generating individual genetic profiles for all rhinoceroses within a protected area provides scope for long-term population monitoring, yielding information on the dispersal of individuals and other parameters required to study the dynamics of a natural population. For large populations, however, such as that of Assam's Kaziranga National Park (. , rhinoceroses according to a total count census conducted by Assam Forest Department in ), sampling strategies need to be developed further to facilitate the use of genetic tools for population monitoring.
Genetic monitoring can provide information on various aspects of genetic diversity, but for regular monitoring purposes the traditional total count method is easier for forest departments to implement. This is primarily because of the need for technical expertise and laboratory facilities rather than because of the costs involved. We recommend a multidisciplinary approach to monitoring populations of greater one-horned rhinoceros in India, based on a combination of traditional and advanced ecological and genetic monitoring techniques, to provide the necessary data for conservation management of the species in situ.

AT participated in the collection of reference tissue samples. BKT contributed towards research planning and collection of reference samples.
